parts.label: energy-flow
parts.display_text: Construct an energy-flow diagram from incoming solar radiation to electricity generated by a wind turbine. Indicate where energy is transferred to less useful forms.

answer.text: Solar radiation → uneven heating of Earth and atmosphere → kinetic energy of moving air → rotational kinetic energy of turbine → electrical energy. Thermal energy is dispersed during heating, friction and electrical resistance; some wind energy passes the turbine.

parts.label: a
parts.display_text: Describe the energy transformations in a tidal-barrage power system.

answer.text: A difference in water level stores gravitational potential energy. Water flowing through a turbine transfers energy to rotation, and the generator converts some of this into electricity.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: b
parts.display_text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of generating electricity with a tidal barrage.

answer.text: Tides are predictable and no fuel is burned during operation. Generation is intermittent and suitable sites are limited; construction can also disrupt estuarine ecosystems.

parts.label: c
parts.display_text: A tidal basin covers 1.0 × 10⁶ m² with a tidal range of 4.0 m. Water density is 1000 kg m⁻³. Estimate the gravitational energy available per tide and the maximum daily mean power for two generating tides per day.

answer.text: The average head is h/2, so E = ½ρAgh² ≈ 7.8 × 10¹⁰ J per tide. Maximum daily mean power = 2E/86400 ≈ 1.8 MW. Useful mean power is lower and requires an efficiency factor.

parts.label: a
parts.display_text: Explain how a tidal dam with valves, water passages, a turbine and a generator can produce electricity.

answer.text: Close the gates while the tide changes to establish a height difference across the dam. Open a turbine passage so water flows through and drives the generator. Reverse-flow or separate passages can permit generation on the opposite tide.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: b
parts.display_text: Give two factors limiting the widespread use of tidal-barrage electricity generation.

answer.text: A sufficiently large tidal range and suitable enclosed coastline are needed. Dams are expensive and can disrupt habitats and navigation; generation also varies over the tidal cycle.

parts.label: c.i
parts.display_text: Identify the gravitational origin of Earth’s tides.

answer.text: The Moon’s gravitational field, and to a lesser extent the Sun’s, varies across Earth. These differences produce tidal effects.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: c.ii
parts.display_text: Tidal power ultimately draws on mechanical energy in the Earth–Moon system, chiefly Earth’s rotation. Explain whether it provides energy “for nothing” and whether that store is unlimited.

answer.text: It converts existing mechanical energy rather than creating energy. Extraction contributes to an extremely small reduction in Earth’s rotational energy. The store is finite, though enormous on human timescales.

At terminal speed the upward drag equals mg. In time t the object moves distance vt, so the work transferred to the air is force times distance = mg(vt) = mgvt. Therefore A.
